newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Federal Reserve keeps interest rates steady.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Federal Reserve keeps interest rates steady.

text.p: By Rich Miller, Economics Correspondent
The U.S. Federal Reserve held off from increasing interest rates on Tuesday in what analysts described as a calculated gamble that the economy will slow before inflation starts to rise.
"Instead of raising rates, they've crossed their fingers," said Robert Brusca, chief economist for Wall Street broker Nikko Securities Inc.
President Clinton hailed the central bank's decision, saying it showed that the economy was on track.
"I just think it shows we've got a strong economy with no inflation. I'm glad about that," Clinton told reporters during a campaign visit to New Jersey.
The decision was good news for Clinton, who has been counting on a trouble-free economy in the run-up to the Nov. 5 election to help him win a second, four-year term.

Wall Street's reaction was mixed. After surging in the immediate wake of the Fed announcement, share prices fell back on profit-taking following their recent record run. The Dow Jones industrial average closed 20.71 points lower at 5,874.
Bond prices gained, with the pace-setting 30-year Treasury issue jumping nearly a half point, pushing the yield down to 6.98 percent from 7.02 percent Monday.
Many analysts still expect the Fed to raise interest rates sometime in the coming months, possibly at its next policy meeting on Nov. 13 -- eight days after the election.
"If it hadn't been for the election, they probably would have raised rates," said David Wyss, of Massachusetts-based consultants DRI/McGraw Hill.
As is its wont, the secretive Fed did not formally announce its decision to hold rates steady, but instead merely said that it had ended its meeting after 4-1/2 hours of talks.
"The Federal Open Market Committee meeting ended at 1:40 p.m. (1740 GMT)," central bank spokesman Joseph Coyne said. "There is no further announcement."
The bland statement hid what analysts believed was one of the more contentious meetings of the policy-making committee.
Anti-inflation hawks at the Fed, particularly at its regional banks, have made no secret of their desire for higher rates to cool off the economy and head off inflation.
Tuesday's decision left the federal funds rate that banks charge each other for overnight money at 5-1/4 percent and the discount rate the Fed charges banks for loans at five percent.
The central bank has not changed either rate since Jan. 31, when it cut them both by a quarter percentage point.
Fed policymakers were faced with conflicting evidence on the state of the economy when they met on Tuesday.
By opting not to raise rates now, the Fed is hoping that economic growth will slow down enough on its own to head off the risk of higher inflation, analysts said.
In the words of Fed Governor Janet Yellen, the economy is operating in an "inflationary danger zone." But so far there is no clear sign of higher inflation.
At 5.1 percent, the unemployment rate is at its lowest point in more than seven years and at a level that in the past has often led to stepped-up wage demands and higher inflation.
Wages, in fact, have already begun to pick up. But so far companies have been unable to pass through those higher labour costs to consumers in the form of price increases.
Much will depend on the future course of the economy.

In the second quarter, the economy grew at a 4.8 percent clip -- its fastest pace in two years and about twice the rate most analysts reckon is sustainable on a long-term basis without fanning inflation.
Growth has slowed since then, as consumer spending, which accounts for about two-thirds of the economy, has slackened.

But with consumer confidence at about a six-year high, labour markets tight and wages rising, some analysts -- and Fed anti-inflation hawks -- question whether the slowdown that is on its way will be enough to keep price pressures in check.
The central bank was under considerable political pressure not to raise rates Tuesday, six weeks ahead of the election.
Seventy eight lawmakers -- all but two of them Democrats -- wrote to Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan on Monday contending that a rate rise now would hurt, not help the economy.
And Clinton administration officials have argued that inflation remained quiescent, strongly implying that they saw no need for the independent central bank to raise rates.
